title: Embeddings and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
monthTitle: Generative AI and LLM Foundations for Data Scientists
summary: Learn how text embeddings turn documents into dense vectors where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness, and how to use them to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. This lesson walks from generating embeddings with Voyage AI, through semantic search with cosine similarity, to grounding an LLM's answers in retrieved context so it responds from your data rather than its training memory.
objectives: Explain what text embeddings are and why semantic similarity maps to geometric closeness
Generate document and query embeddings using the Voyage AI client
Implement semantic search with cosine similarity using only numpy
Build a minimal RAG pipeline that retrieves top-k chunks and grounds an LLM answer in them
Choose when to scale from in-memory search to a vector database like Chroma or pgvector
Evaluate when RAG helps, when retrieval quality limits it, and how the pattern stays provider-agnostic

quiz.q: What does a text embedding actually represent?
options: A compressed copy of the original text that can be decoded back to words
A hash that is identical only for identical strings
A dense vector of numbers positioning the text in a space where similar meanings sit close together
The model's final answer to a question about the text
quiz.why: An embedding is a dense numeric vector. Semantically similar texts land near each other geometrically, which is exactly what makes vector-based semantic search work. It is not a reversible compression or a hash.

quiz.q: Which provider does this lesson use for embeddings, and why not Anthropic?
options: Voyage AI, because Anthropic offers no embeddings API and recommends Voyage
Anthropic, via its dedicated embeddings endpoint
Anthropic, by asking Claude to output a vector
Any LLM, since every chat model also returns embeddings
quiz.why: Anthropic does not provide an embeddings API; it officially recommends Voyage AI. You call vo.embed(...) with VOYAGE_API_KEY. Chat models like Claude generate text, not embedding vectors.

quiz.q: In semantic search, why is cosine similarity a natural choice for comparing two embedding vectors?
options: It counts how many words two texts share
It only works after the vectors are sorted
It requires the vectors to be integers
It measures the angle between vectors, so it captures directional (semantic) similarity regardless of magnitude
quiz.why: Cosine similarity is the normalized dot product: it measures the angle between vectors, capturing how aligned their directions are independent of length. That aligns with how embedding models encode meaning as direction.

quiz.q: In a RAG pipeline, what is the role of the retrieved top-k chunks?
options: They are used to fine-tune the model's weights at request time
They are inserted into the prompt as context so the model answers grounded in them
They replace the user's question entirely
They are discarded after retrieval and only the scores are sent to the model
quiz.why: RAG retrieves the most relevant chunks and places them in the prompt as context. The model is then instructed to answer using that context, which grounds the response in your data and reduces hallucination. No weights are updated.

quiz.q: When should you move from in-memory numpy cosine search to a vector database such as Chroma or pgvector?
options: As soon as you have more than one document
Only when you switch embedding providers
When the corpus grows large enough that scanning every vector per query becomes too slow or memory-heavy
Never, because numpy always outperforms a vector database
quiz.why: A brute-force numpy scan is fine for small corpora but recomputes similarity against every vector each query. Vector databases add indexing, persistence, and approximate nearest-neighbor search that scale to large corpora.

quiz.q: Open-ended: Describe the limits of RAG. Why is retrieval quality often called the ceiling of a RAG system, and name two things you could change to raise that ceiling.
quiz.why: RAG end-to-end quality is capped by what retrieval finds — the generator cannot use information it never receives.
quiz.answer: Retrieval quality is the ceiling because the LLM can only ground its answer in the chunks retrieval actually surfaces — if the relevant chunk is never retrieved, no amount of model capability recovers it. Two things you could change to raise that ceiling: improve the chunking strategy and use a stronger or domain-tuned embedding model (other options: query rewriting, re-ranking or increasing top-k, and improving corpus coverage/freshness).

body_markdown:
## What Embeddings Are

An **embedding** turns a piece of text into a **dense vector** of floating-point numbers, often hundreds or thousands of dimensions. The key property: the model is trained so that texts with similar *meaning* land close together in this space, while unrelated texts land far apart. Semantic similarity becomes **geometric closeness**.

That is what makes embeddings useful. Instead of matching keywords, you ask "which document is most like this query?" and answer with arithmetic. "How do I reset my password?" and "I forgot my login credentials" share almost no words, yet their embeddings sit near each other because they mean nearly the same thing.

## Generating Embeddings

A crucial accuracy point: **Anthropic does not offer an embeddings API.** For embeddings, Anthropic officially recommends **Voyage AI**. Newer Voyage models may exist, so check the docs.

```python
import voyageai

vo = voyageai.Client()  # reads VOYAGE_API_KEY

result = vo.embed(documents, model="voyage-3.5",
                  input_type="document")
vectors = result.embeddings  # list[list[float]]
```

Use `input_type="document"` for your corpus and `input_type="query"` for a user's search query. The pattern is **provider-agnostic** — open-source models such as **BGE** or **E5** produce comparable vectors, and the retrieval logic does not change.

## Semantic Search with Cosine Similarity

Once text is vectors, finding the closest matches is just math. **Cosine similarity** measures the angle between two vectors — the normalized dot product — so it captures directional (semantic) alignment regardless of magnitude. Pure numpy is enough:

```python
import numpy as np

def cosine(a, b):
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b)
    return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

def top_k(query_vec, doc_vecs, k=3):
    scores = [cosine(query_vec, d) for d in doc_vecs]
    ranked = sorted(enumerate(scores),
                    key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    return ranked[:k]  # [(index, score), ...]
```

Embed the query with `input_type="query"`, score it against the stored vectors, and take the highest few. This dependency-light approach is perfect for learning and small corpora.

## From Search to RAG

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation** joins that search step to a language model: **retrieve** the top-k relevant chunks, **augment** the prompt by inserting them as context, and **generate** an answer grounded in them.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
q = vo.embed([question], model="voyage-3.5",
             input_type="query").embeddings[0]
context = "\n".join(docs[i] for i, _ in top_k(q, vectors))

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8", max_tokens=1024,
    system=("Answer ONLY using the provided context. "
            "If it's not there, say you don't know."),
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"}])
answer = msg.content[0].text
```

We use the stable Anthropic Messages API for generation. The system instruction is doing real work: it tells the model to stay inside the retrieved context and admit ignorance rather than invent an answer. Default to Claude, but learn model selection for your latency and cost needs. Never `eval()` model output.

## Scaling Up with Vector Databases

The numpy scan recomputes cosine similarity against *every* vector each query — fine for hundreds of chunks, but it breaks down as the corpus grows. A **vector database** adds persistence, indexing, and approximate nearest-neighbor search so queries stay fast at scale.

```python
import chromadb

collection = chromadb.Client().create_collection("docs")
collection.add(ids=ids, embeddings=vectors,
               documents=documents)
hits = collection.query(query_embeddings=[q], n_results=3)
```

**Chroma** is a lightweight place to start; **pgvector** keeps vectors right inside Postgres alongside your relational data. The retrieval interface changes, but the RAG pattern is identical.

## When RAG Helps — and Its Limits

RAG shines when you need answers **grounded in your own data**: private knowledge bases, fresh information past the model's training cutoff, or domains where hallucination is costly. By forcing the model to answer from retrieved context, you make responses traceable and far more trustworthy.

But RAG has a ceiling: **retrieval quality.** If the relevant chunk is never retrieved, no model can recover it. Raising that ceiling means better chunking, a stronger embedding model, query rewriting, re-ranking, and good corpus coverage. Build the retrieval well, and the generation takes care of itself.

In this lesson we connect two ideas every data scientist working with language models needs: embeddings, which turn text into vectors where meaning becomes distance, and retrieval-augmented generation, which uses those vectors to ground a model's answers in your own data. We'll build the whole pipeline from embedding to retrieval to grounded generation.

slides.title: When RAG Helps
bullets: Grounds answers in your own private or domain data
Brings in fresh knowledge past the model's training cutoff
Reduces hallucination by forcing answers from retrieved context
Makes responses traceable back to source chunks
slides.narration: RAG shines when you need answers grounded in your own data: private knowledge bases, information newer than the model's training cutoff, or domains where a made-up answer is costly. By forcing the model to answer from retrieved context, you make its responses traceable and far more trustworthy. This is the core reason RAG has become the default way to put an LLM to work over a specific body of knowledge.

slides.title: The Limits of RAG
bullets: Retrieval quality is the ceiling on answer quality
If the right chunk is never retrieved, no model can recover it
Raise the ceiling: better chunking, stronger embeddings, re-ranking
Also: query rewriting and good corpus coverage and freshness
slides.narration: RAG has one hard limit worth internalizing: retrieval quality is the ceiling. If the relevant chunk is never retrieved, the model cannot answer correctly no matter how capable it is. So the leverage is mostly in retrieval, not generation. Raise that ceiling with better chunking, a stronger or domain-tuned embedding model, query rewriting, re-ranking the results, and good corpus coverage and freshness. Build the retrieval well, and the generation takes care of itself.
